group.line: A 401 reply leads to metadata files, a client is recognised by its metadata page, registration or a fixed entry, and the token is checked for audience, PKCE and issuer.
group.dumb: An AI client knocks on the brain's door and is told where to sign in. The sign-in server works out which client it is. The user logs in once, and the ticket it gets works only at this door. If a question needs an app the user has not linked, the brain sends them to its own page for that.

cl_meta.line:
401 reply names resource_metadata URL (RFC 9728); server metadata at RFC 8414 well-known path
client reads both, then signs in
cl_meta.dumb: When an AI client calls the brain without a login, the brain answers 401 and says where to read a small public file. That file names the sign-in server. A second small file on the sign-in server lists its login and token addresses. The client needs no hand-typed settings.
cl_meta.inn: An HTTP request to the MCP endpoint with no valid bearer token, or a GET to /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource. Fields used: Host, path, Authorization header (absent or invalid).
cl_meta.out: 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer header carrying resource_metadata=<URL>. The protected resource document {resource, authorization_servers[], scopes_supported, bearer_methods_supported}. The sign-in server document {issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, registration_endpoint?, code_challenge_methods_supported}.
cl_meta.store: Reads the tenant host map and the sign-in server's issuer URL from config. Writes nothing per request. Both documents are static JSON served with a 5 minute Cache-Control (design).
cl_meta.fail: If the metadata file cannot be built (issuer unset), the MCP endpoint refuses to start rather than serve a bad 401. A client that gets a 404 on the file retries once after 2 s then shows its own manual-config prompt (client behaviour, not ours). Any metadata fetch that takes over 3 s counts as failed and the health check turns red after 3 misses in 60 s (design).
cl_meta.req: Requirement: 'discovers the auth server through RFC 9728 protected resource metadata'
cl_meta.hard: The exact field list comes from the two RFCs and the MCP authorization page (status fetched); the MCP roadmap names a Server Card working group for .well-known metadata that may add a third file. Not yet decided: one metadata set per tenant host or one global set.
cl_meta.prop: Proposal: five different clients must find the sign-in server alone, so the 401 reply and two public files are the single place that tells them, instead of five hand-written setup guides.

deep.purpose: Let any MCP client learn where to sign in from the first 401 reply, so rollout needs only the server URL and no per-client auth settings.
expected: An unauthenticated POST to /mcp returns 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header with a resource_metadata URL that returns 200 JSON
The resource field in the protected resource document equals the exact MCP endpoint URL that clients type in
Every URL in the sign-in server document uses https and the same issuer string as the iss claim in tokens
not_expected: It does not issue tokens or register clients; the sign-in server (cl_reg) does
It does not accept a token in a query string or give any hint about which users exist

algorithm.name: Discovery by 401 challenge (RFC 9728) then server metadata (RFC 8414)
steps: On a request with no valid token, return 401 and set WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://<host>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"
Serve the protected resource document with resource set to the canonical MCP URL and authorization_servers set to the sign-in server issuer
On the sign-in server, serve the RFC 8414 document at its well-known path with code_challenge_methods_supported = ["S256"] only
Add a startup self-check that fetches both documents through the public URL and compares resource and issuer with config

params.cache_control: max-age=300 (design): short enough that an issuer change spreads within 5 minutes
params.scopes_supported: brain.read only (design): the brain exposes no write tool, see ll_ro
params.bearer_methods_supported: header only, per the MCP authorization page (t_t24)

alternatives.name: Hand-written config per client
alternatives.why_rejected: Five clients, five config shapes, and every issuer change breaks them all; discovery fixes it once.

alternatives.name: Skip metadata and hard-code the issuer in each client config
alternatives.why_rejected: Cursor and Gemini CLI both discover through the 401 reply per clients.json; hard-coding adds a failure mode they do not need.

security: Metadata spoofing: an attacker who controls DNS or a proxy could point clients at a fake sign-in server; control is https only, HSTS, and the startup self-check that compares issuer with config
Information leak: the 401 body must not say whether a token was expired, wrong audience or unknown; it returns one generic error so a prober learns nothing about token state

performance.slo: p99 under 50 ms for the 401 and both documents (static JSON, design)
performance.complexity: O(1) per request, no store read
performance.scaling: At 10x load the documents sit behind the CDN with the 5 minute cache; the 401 path is a single header check and needs no database.

edge_cases: A request with a malformed Authorization header: treated as no token, same 401, no stack trace
Issuer URL with a trailing slash versus without: normalise once at startup; mismatch fails the self-check
Two tenants on two hostnames: one protected resource document per host, so resource always matches the host the client used
A new app joins through the connector manifest (so_sdk) or the MCP bridge (so_mcp); neither touches discovery because discovery describes only the brain's own front door

tests.name: 401 carries pointer
tests.expect: status 401 and header WWW-Authenticate contains resource_metadata=https://

cost_levers: Static documents behind a CDN make discovery cost near zero per client sign-in
feedback_events: A spike of 401 followed by no sign-in from one client family flags a discovery bug for that client

analytics_events.name: auth.discovery
analytics_events.when: on every 401 and every metadata GET

papers.key_idea: MCP authorization is built on RFC 9728 protected resource metadata and RFC 8414 server metadata so clients find the sign-in server themselves.
papers.how: We serve exactly those two documents and nothing custom.

repos.name: FastMCP
repos.take: Its HTTP auth helpers can serve the protected resource document; check current docs for the version that exposes it.

deep.industry: Cursor discovers the auth server through RFC 9728 and Gemini CLI auto-discovers after a 401 (clients.json, both fetched). Glean serves one MCP URL per tenant that works for any host.

cl_reg.line:
Client ID metadata document (https client_id) first, dynamic registration fallback, static client last
issuer-bound
cl_reg.dumb: Before a client can sign in, the sign-in server must know who it is. The preferred way is that the client's ID is a web address, and the server reads a small file there that lists its allowed return addresses. Older clients register themselves instead. A few hosts use a fixed, pre-agreed ID.
cl_reg.inn: An authorization request with client_id and redirect_uri. If client_id starts with https:// it is a metadata document URL. Otherwise it is a registered id. Also a POST to the registration endpoint {client_name, redirect_uris[], application_type, token_endpoint_auth_method}.
cl_reg.out: A client record {client_id, kind: cimd|dcr|static, redirect_uris[], issuer, first_seen, status} handed to the token audience check (cl_aud), or an error invalid_client.
cl_reg.store: Reads and writes the client table in the sign-in server's database (one row per client, keyed by client_id). Caches fetched metadata documents with their expiry time. Static clients come from a config file in version control.
cl_reg.fail: A metadata document fetch that times out at 3 s (design), returns over 5 KB (design), or is not https is rejected with invalid_client; no retry inside the sign-in request, the client may try again. A registration flood over 20 per hour per IP (design) returns 429 for 1 hour.
cl_reg.req: Requirement: 'credentials bound to issuer; DCR formally deprecated in favor of CIMD'
cl_reg.hard: Open: whether admins approve new clients per tenant or the brain accepts any client that proves its redirect URI. Slack-style hosts need a static client with a fixed app id and no registration (clients.json, fetched), so the static table must exist even if CIMD is the default. ChatGPT admin detail is snippet level only.
cl_reg.prop: Proposal: clients differ (Codex and ChatGPT support the metadata document, Claude.ai offers published identity or automatic registration, Cursor and others use dynamic or static), so the server accepts all three and prefers the safest.

deep.purpose: Recognise every AI client with the safest method it supports, so a new client joins without an admin editing a shared secret.
expected: A client whose client_id is an https URL with a valid metadata document is accepted without prior registration
A client that registers dynamically gets a client_id bound to this issuer and cannot use it at another sign-in server
A static client named in config signs in with its fixed id and fixed redirect URLs
not_expected: It does not grant access; it only says who the client is, and cl_aud and per-user consent decide the rest
It does not accept a redirect_uri that is not listed exactly in the client record

algorithm.name: Client resolution order: metadata document, then registered, then static
algorithm.formula: kind(client_id) = cimd if client_id is an https URL; dcr if found in client table; static if found in config; else reject
steps: If client_id is an https URL, fetch it with a 3 s timeout, 5 KB cap, no redirects, and block private and link-local addresses
Check the document's client_id equals the URL it was fetched from and redirect_uri in the request is in its redirect_uris list by exact match
Else look up the id in the client table (dynamic registration rows), then in the static client config
Store the resolved record with the issuer, and cache a metadata document for the shorter of its Cache-Control and 1 hour (design)

params.registration_rate: 20 per IP per hour (design); tune from abuse logs

alternatives.name: Dynamic registration only
alternatives.why_rejected: The 2026-07-28 spec deprecates it in favour of the metadata document and it creates one row per client install.

alternatives.name: One shared static client for every host
alternatives.why_rejected: Slack-style and Cursor static OAuth need fixed redirect URLs, but one shared secret across clients cannot be revoked per client.

security: Server-side request forgery through the metadata URL: attacker sets client_id to http://169.254.169.254/ ; control is https only, block private and link-local ranges after DNS resolution, no redirects, 5 KB cap
Open redirect and code theft through a lax redirect_uri: control is exact string match against the stored list, and loopback ports handled per the spec's native-app rule (check current docs)
Client impersonation: a page that copies a famous client's metadata URL cannot receive the code because the redirect list lives in the document served from the real domain

performance.slo: p95 under 150 ms for a cached client, under 500 ms with a cold metadata fetch (design)
performance.complexity: O(1) table lookup; one outbound HTTP fetch on a cache miss
performance.scaling: At 10x sign-ins the cold fetch is the cost; the cache keyed by client_id removes repeat fetches, and the per-IP limit stops fetch floods.

edge_cases: Same client_id from two tenants: the client record is global, consent is per user and tenant
Metadata document changes its redirect_uris: the next fetch after the cache expires replaces the list; in-flight codes keep the old list
Document unreachable: reject, never fall back to a guessed redirect
Unicode or very long client_name: store as given up to 200 chars, escape on the admin screen
A new AI client joins by publishing a metadata document; no change to the brain or its manifest is needed. A new source app is unrelated and joins through so_sdk or so_mcp

tests.name: cimd accepted
tests.given: client_id https://client.example/meta.json whose doc lists redirect http://127.0.0.1:33418/cb
tests.expect: authorization proceeds; client record kind = cimd

tests.name: ssrf blocked
tests.expect: invalid_client and no outbound request made

tests.name: redirect mismatch
tests.given: valid client, redirect_uri not in list

cost_levers: Caching metadata documents; one table row per dynamic client is the only storage cost
feedback_events: Admin marks a client as untrusted; its record status flips to blocked and its tokens are revoked

papers.key_idea: The MCP authorization page lists RFC 7591 dynamic registration and OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents as the supported ways to identify a client.
papers.how: We implement the metadata document first and keep registration as fallback.

deep.industry: ChatGPT recommends Client ID Metadata Documents where supported, Codex supports them and dynamic registration, Slack allows neither dynamic registration nor a self-chosen id (clients.json, fetched). Linear and Sourcegraph use dynamic registration.

cl_aud.line:
PKCE S256 + RFC 8707 resource checked as token audience + RFC 9207 iss in redirect
accept = sig and aud = this URL and exp
cl_aud.dumb: A token is only a ticket for one door. The brain checks that the ticket was issued for this server and no other, that it has not expired, and that the sign-in used a one-time secret so a thief cannot swap the code. The sign-in server also says who it is in the return address so a client is not tricked into using a fake one.
cl_aud.inn: Authorization request {client_id, redirect_uri, code_challenge, code_challenge_method, resource, state}, token request {code, code_verifier, resource}, and later the bearer JWT on each MCP call.
cl_aud.out: On sign-in: an authorization code, then an access token whose aud equals the MCP resource URL, redirect carrying iss. On each call: accept with the user id and scope, or 401.
cl_aud.store: Reads signing keys (JWKS) and the canonical resource URL from config. Stores each pending code with its code_challenge for 60 s (design). No token is stored by the resource server.
cl_aud.fail: Wrong audience, expired, bad signature, or missing resource: 401 at once, no retry. Code replay: second use of a code revokes the tokens already issued from it. JWKS fetch failure: serve from the cached key set for up to 10 minutes (design), then fail closed with 503.
cl_aud.req: Requirement: 'servers must validate audience and must not pass the client's token upstream'
cl_aud.hard: The exact RFC 8707 wording was marked snippet in clients.json (exact quotes not extracted), so the audience rule here follows the MCP authorization page summary. Open: access token lifetime (default 15 minutes proposed, tune from refresh traffic).
cl_aud.prop: Proposal: a stolen or mis-sent token must be useless anywhere except at this server, so audience, PKCE and issuer checks form one gate in front of every tool call.

deep.purpose: Make a token valid only for this brain and only for the user who signed in, and make the sign-in itself safe against code theft and fake sign-in servers.
expected: A token issued with resource = https://brain.example.com/mcp is accepted there and rejected at any other server
A sign-in without a valid code_verifier for the stored S256 challenge fails
The redirect carries iss, and a client that sees a different iss than the one it started with refuses the code
not_expected: It does not decide which tools a user may call; scope checks and ll_quota do
It never forwards the inbound token to a source app; downstream calls use an exchanged token (so_obo)

algorithm.name: PKCE S256 plus audience-bound token validation
algorithm.formula: accept(call) = verify_sig(jwt) and jwt.aud contains RESOURCE and jwt.exp > now and jwt.iss = ISSUER and challenge = base64url(sha256(verifier))
steps: At authorization, require code_challenge with method S256 and the resource parameter equal to the canonical MCP URL; reject plain
At the token request, recompute base64url(sha256(code_verifier)) and compare with the stored challenge in constant time
Mint the access token with aud = resource and a short life; add iss to the authorization redirect
On each MCP call, read the bearer from the Authorization header only, verify signature, iss, exp and that aud contains this server's URL
Reject the call and write a deny audit row on any failed check

params.code_ttl_s: 60 (design); one browser round trip is a few seconds

definitions: verifier: 43 to 128 random characters the client keeps secret
aud: audience claim in the token
skew: allowed clock difference in seconds
math.formula_full: challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(ASCII(verifier))); accept iff aud contains RESOURCE and now - skew <= exp
math.derivation: The server stores only the hash. An attacker who steals the code cannot produce the verifier because sha256 cannot be reversed in practice, so the code alone is worthless. Binding aud stops a token minted for another server from being replayed here.
math.worked_example: verifier = 43 random characters from a 66-symbol alphabet gives 66^43 about 2^260 possibilities, above the 2^256 hash output, so guessing the verifier is not easier than breaking the hash. Token exp = 12:15:00, now = 12:15:20, skew 30 s: still accepted for 10 more seconds; at 12:15:31 rejected.
math.complexity: O(1): one hash, one signature verify (about 0.1 ms for ES256 on a laptop class CPU, tune with a benchmark).
failure_modes: A server that checks signature but not aud accepts tokens meant for other services; the test below covers it
Clock drift above skew rejects good tokens; alert when 401 for expired rises above 2 percent
math.calibration: Keep access_ttl_s at 900 until refresh calls exceed 30 percent of traffic, then raise to 1800 only with security review.

alternatives.name: Opaque tokens with introspection
alternatives.why_rejected: Adds a network call to the sign-in server on every tool call; signed JWTs with aud avoid it, revocation is handled by a short life plus ac_neg.

alternatives.name: Accept any token from the trusted issuer
alternatives.why_rejected: Removes the audience check and allows confused-deputy replay across services.

security: Confused deputy and token passthrough: a token issued for another service replayed here, or this token forwarded upstream; control is the aud check here and an exchanged token downstream
Authorization code interception on a loopback or custom redirect: control is PKCE S256 so the stolen code needs the verifier

Mix-up attack: a malicious sign-in server returns a code to a client that thinks it came from the real one; control is the iss value in the redirect, validated by the client (RFC 9207, listed in the 2026-07-28 changes)
Token in a URL leaks into logs; control is header-only transport and a log scrubber for the Authorization header

performance.slo: p99 under 5 ms added per tool call (design)
performance.complexity: O(1) per call with a cached JWKS
performance.scaling: At 10x calls the key fetch could become a bottleneck; keep the key set in memory and refresh every 10 minutes or on an unknown kid.

edge_cases: Token with aud as an array: pass if our URL is one element
Resource URL with and without trailing slash: canonicalise once, compare exact
Unknown kid after key rotation: refetch the key set once, then reject
Two quick uses of the same code: first wins, second revokes the family
A new AI client or source app needs no change here; audience is always the brain's own URL

tests.name: pkce mismatch
tests.given: token request with a different verifier

tests.name: iss in redirect
tests.expect: query contains iss equal to the metadata issuer

cost_levers: Stateless JWT checks avoid a per-call round trip to the sign-in server
feedback_events: A deny audit row with reason aud_mismatch for a known client raises a ticket to check its resource setting

papers.key_idea: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE S256, RFC 8707 resource parameter, servers validate audience and never pass the client's token to another service.
papers.how: All three are gates in the algorithm above.

repos.name: agentgateway
repos.take: A policy proxy that can enforce token checks in front of the MCP server; we take the idea of one enforcement point.

deep.industry: Slack's MCP server uses PKCE for desktop clients and user tokens with per-tool scopes (t_t25). Gemini CLI validates the RFC 9207 iss value (clients.json, fetched).

cl_consent.line:
URL-mode elicitation: tool returns a link to the brain's own consent page when a source is unlinked
state bound to user
cl_consent.dumb: Sometimes a person asks a question that needs an app they have not linked yet. The brain does not ask for passwords in the chat. It sends the client a link to its own page, the person links the app there, and then the question is asked again.
cl_consent.inn: A tool call from ll_mcp that needs source app X for user U, where U has no stored link for X. Fields: tenant_id, user_id, source_id, requested scopes.
cl_consent.out: An elicitation request in url mode {mode: url, message, url} with a one-time link {state, expires}, then the user's action accept, decline or cancel. After accept and the link completing, the original call is retried.
cl_consent.store: Writes a pending-link row {state, user_id, source_id, expires_at, used} for 10 minutes (design). Reads the user's link status from the token vault (so_oauth). Never stores a source credential here.
cl_consent.fail: User declines or cancels: the tool returns results from linked sources only plus a note naming the unlinked source. Link not completed in 10 minutes (design): the state row expires and a fresh call makes a new link. Client without elicitation support: the tool returns the same link as plain text in the tool result.
cl_consent.req: Requirement: 'url (out-of-band, for credentials and third-party OAuth)'
cl_consent.hard: The 2026-07-28 spec moves elicitation into multi round-trip requests (InputRequiredResult); the exact reply shape must be checked in the spec, and each client's support is uneven (Cursor and Claude Code list elicitation; others were not confirmed in clients.json). Wording per client has not been user-tested.
cl_consent.prop: Proposal: a missing source link is the most common first-run failure, so the brain turns it into a guided step in the client instead of a silent empty answer.

deep.purpose: When a source app is not linked for this user, send them to the brain's consent page out of band so credentials never pass through the chat or the AI client.
expected: A search that needs an unlinked source returns a url-mode elicitation instead of an empty result
After the user links the app, repeating the call returns results from that app without another prompt
The link works once, only for the user it was made for, and only before it expires
not_expected: It never uses form mode to collect a password, token or API key
It does not let an admin link on behalf of a user; admin app consent is so_admin

algorithm.name: URL-mode elicitation with a bound one-time state
algorithm.formula: link = https://<host>/connect?state=HMAC(user_id, source_id, nonce, expiry); valid iff not used and now < expiry and session_user = state.user_id
steps: ll_mcp reports an unlinked source for the call; build a state value from user_id, source_id, a random nonce and a 10 minute expiry, signed with a server key
Return an elicitation request with mode url and the consent page link; the client shows it and asks the user to open it
On the consent page, require the user to be signed in as the same user, then start the source app's own OAuth through so_oauth
Mark the state used on success and tell the client the elicitation is complete; if the user answers decline or cancel, return partial results with a note

params.state_ttl_s: 600 (design): long enough for an app's own login and two-factor prompt
params.retry_after_link: client repeats the original call; no server push (design)

alternatives.name: Form mode asking for an API key
alternatives.why_rejected: The elicitation page says form mode is never for secrets; keys would pass through the AI client and its logs.

alternatives.name: Return an error text with a link only
alternatives.why_rejected: Works everywhere but gives no structured accept or decline; kept as the fallback for clients without elicitation.

security: Phishing through the link: attacker sends a victim a link built for the attacker's account; control is binding state to the signed-in session user and showing the source app name and scopes on the page
Open redirect and replay of state: control is single use, 10 minute expiry, HMAC signature and exact redirect to the brain host only
Approval fatigue: repeated prompts train users to click through; control is at most one prompt per user per source per hour (design)

performance.slo: link built in under 20 ms; whole link flow depends on the user, tracked as median seconds to complete (target under 60 s, design)
performance.scaling: At 10x users the prompt rate is bounded by the once-per-hour limit and the state table is purged by expiry.

edge_cases: Two parallel calls both need source X: one pending state per user and source; the second call reuses it
User links the app on another device: state is not tied to the device, only to the user session
Source link exists but token revoked: treated as unlinked and prompts again
Unicode source names: shown as given, escaped in HTML
A new source joins through so_sdk or so_mcp and appears in this prompt as soon as its manifest names an OAuth flow
The consent screen names the zone each source will feed (company, team or personal) so a person knows which grant they give.

tests.name: prompt on unlinked
tests.given: user U has no link for source drive; call search
tests.expect: reply is an elicitation mode=url with a link on the brain host

tests.name: wrong user
tests.given: state made for U opened in the session of V

cost_levers: Once-per-hour prompt cap and partial results avoid repeated failing calls to unlinked apps
feedback_events: Decline and cancel counts per source feed the admin screen to pre-link or drop a source

papers.key_idea: Third-party credentials must not flow through the MCP client; the server holds its own delegated tokens.
papers.how: URL mode sends the user to our page so the credential never passes the client.

repos.name: Nango
repos.take: Hosts per-user OAuth for many APIs including the link page and token refresh; one option for so_oauth.

deep.industry: The MCP elicitation page says form mode is never for secrets and url mode is for credentials and third-party OAuth (clients.json). Cursor lists elicitation support; Claude Code lists elicitation among its MCP features.
